subject: political-science
readings: OD ch. 5 (Orvis & Drogus, *Governing Institutions in Democracies*)

cards.front: What single question does every system of government answer?
cards.back: **How is executive power organised and held accountable?** That is: how the executive is **chosen**, **checked**, and **removed**. Place each system on Lijphart's **majoritarian** to **consensus** line, measured by the number of **veto players** (Tsebelis).

cards.front: What is the **head of state**?
cards.back: The **symbolic** role of the executive that represents the country, such as a monarch or ceremonial president.

cards.front: What is the **head of government**?
cards.back: The role of the executive that **runs policy and the government**, such as a prime minister, or the president in the US.

cards.front: Which branch of government is essential to every state?
cards.back: The **executive**. The legislature and judiciary exist mainly to **limit** it.
cards.hint: The one branch every state must have.

cards.front: What is a **majoritarian** democracy (Lijphart)?
cards.back: A democracy that **concentrates power**: single party executive dominating the legislature, unicameral, easily amended constitution, so **few veto players** (example: UK).

cards.front: What is a **consensus** democracy (Lijphart)?
cards.back: A democracy that **disperses power**: coalition executives, balanced executive and legislature, bicameral, rigid constitution, so **many veto players** (example: US, Germany).

cards.front: Which concept means any actor whose agreement is needed to change policy?
cards.back: A **veto player**, from **Tsebelis**.

cards.front: According to Tsebelis, what does adding more veto players do to policy?
cards.back: **Less policy change.** More veto players, and greater **ideological distance** between them, shrink the winset, producing gridlock.

cards.front: How does the veto players winset diagram show when a new policy can pass?
cards.back: Each circle is one player's set of policies it prefers to the **status quo**. A policy passes only if it sits inside **every** circle (the **winset** overlap). 1) One player → huge winset. 2) Add players → it shrinks. 3) Enough players → it vanishes → gridlock.
cards.hint: Policy must sit inside every circle.

cards.front: What is **vertical accountability** (O'Donnell)?
cards.back: **Citizens hold the state accountable**, mainly through elections.

cards.front: What is **horizontal accountability** (O'Donnell)?
cards.back: **State institutions check each other**, for example courts striking down a law passed by the legislature.

cards.front: Courts strike down a law passed by parliament. Which type of accountability is this?
cards.back: **Horizontal accountability**: state institutions checking each other, a distinction from **O'Donnell**. (Punishing the government at the ballot box would be **vertical**.)

cards.front: What two independent axes make up Lijphart's map of democracies?
cards.back: 1) **Executives and Parties** axis: consensus (coalitions, balanced) to majoritarian (single party, concentrated). 2) **Federal to Unitary** axis: decentralised to centralised. A democracy is a **point** on both, not one switch. The UK sits far majoritarian; the US is majoritarian and very federal.

cards.front: What defines **parliamentarism** (the Westminster model)?
cards.back: Executive and legislature are **fused**: parliament chooses the chief executive (**PM**), who is both the majority party leader and a sitting legislator.

cards.front: In parliamentarism, is the PM directly elected by citizens?
cards.back: **No.** Citizens vote for **parliament**, and the majority names the PM. A **ceremonial head of state** (monarch or elected president) stays out of politics.
cards.hint: Citizens vote for parliament, not the PM.

cards.front: Which system: powers fused, the chief executive is a party leader sitting in the legislature, removed by no confidence, usually no fixed term?
cards.back: **Parliamentarism** (Westminster). Classic cases: **UK, Germany, India**.

cards.front: How is a PM removed from office in a parliamentary system?
cards.back: By a **vote of no confidence**. The PM then either 1) resigns, so the party picks a new leader, or 2) asks the head of state to call **new elections**. The PM can also **dissolve** parliament. Usually there are no fixed terms.
cards.hint: No confidence → resign or new elections.

cards.front: How often do votes of no confidence succeed?
cards.back: Only about **5%** of the time, but even losing one signals fatal weakness.

cards.front: What makes a PM either very strong or weak?
cards.back: The **party system**. 1) A disciplined **single majority** makes the PM the **most powerful democratic executive in the world**, passing laws almost automatically. 2) **No majority** forces a **coalition**, small parties become veto players, and stability drops (Sweden 2018: 133 days to form a government).

cards.front: What defines **presidentialism**?
cards.back: Executive and legislature are **elected separately with separate powers**: the **separation of powers** (Montesquieu). The defining feature is separation, not that one person leads both roles.

cards.front: How is a president chosen and how long do they serve?
cards.back: The president is **directly elected** and serves a **fixed term**. Branches generally cannot remove each other.

cards.front: Why is it so hard to remove a president?
cards.back: 1) The branches **cannot sack each other**. 2) The only route is a hard **impeachment**. 3) The president holds a **fixed term** regardless of losing support.

cards.front: Why does policymaking stall in presidential systems?
cards.back: Separation of powers means lawmaking needs **both** the president and a legislative majority. These are **built in veto players**. Under **divided government** neither can force the other, producing **gridlock** (example: the US Senate 60 vote filibuster).
cards.hint: Two elected veto players + divided government.

cards.front: What did **Samuels** argue about policy change in presidential systems?
cards.back: They **change the status quo less and more slowly** than parliamentary systems.

cards.front: Which system: separated powers, one directly elected person is both head of state and government, fixed term, removal only by impeachment?
cards.back: **Presidentialism.** Classic cases: **USA, Brazil**.

cards.front: Why is the legislature more powerful in presidential than in parliamentary systems?
cards.back: Under separation of powers a legislator **cannot also sit in the cabinet**, so members have **no ministerial promotion to earn** and stay independent. In parliamentary systems ministers **are** legislators, so ambitious members toe the party line to win cabinet posts, weakening the legislature.
cards.hint: Can a legislator become a minister?

cards.front: What is **coalitional presidentialism**?
cards.back: A presidential system where a **fragmented legislature** forces the president to build an informal **party coalition** and act a little like a PM (classic case: **Brazil**).
cards.hint: President must build a coalition; Brazil.

cards.front: What defines **semi presidentialism**?
cards.back: Executive power is **split**: a **directly elected president** (head of state, real powers) plus a **PM** (head of government) backed by the parliamentary majority.

cards.front: Where and when did semi presidentialism originate?
cards.back: In **France in 1958**, under **de Gaulle**, with the Fifth Republic. It spread from 10 systems in 1990 to 52 in 2018.

cards.front: What is **cohabitation** and what must the president do?
cards.back: Cohabitation is when the president and the legislative majority come from **different parties**. The president must appoint a **PM from the opposing majority** and retreat to their own domain. French norm: 1) the president runs foreign policy and defence, 2) the PM runs domestic policy.

cards.front: What is **Elgie's** key question for judging a semi presidential system?
cards.back: **Can the president dismiss the PM?** If yes, unstable (Russia). If no, genuine power sharing, as stable as parliamentarism (France).
cards.hint: Can the president fire the PM?

cards.front: Which system: a directly elected president with real powers plus a PM answerable to parliament, where cohabitation is possible?
cards.back: **Semi presidentialism** (the split executive). Classic cases: **France, Russia**.

cards.front: Compare parliamentary, presidential, and semi presidential systems on powers, how the executive is chosen, removal, and veto players.
cards.back: **Powers:** fused · separated · split. **Chosen:** parliament names PM · directly elected · president elected, PM by parliament. **Removed:** no confidence · impeachment only · PM by no confidence, president fixed. **Veto players:** few · built in · depends. **Cases:** UK · USA · France.

cards.front: How do parliamentary and presidential systems differ on accountability?
cards.back: 1) **Parliamentarism:** clearest **vertical** accountability (voters know whom to blame) but a weak **horizontal** check under a single majority. 2) **Presidentialism:** strong **horizontal** accountability (separation of powers) but this can hurt effective policymaking.

cards.front: Who argued that presidentialism is inherently crisis prone, and in what work?
cards.back: **Linz**, in **The Perils of Presidentialism** (1990).

cards.front: What are Linz's three perils of presidentialism?
cards.back: 1) **Dual legitimacy:** two independently elected branches with no democratic tie breaker. 2) **Winner take all:** presidents over read their mandate and refuse to compromise. 3) **Inflexible fixed terms:** a failing president cannot be removed. Danger peaks for new democracies under coalitional presidentialism.
cards.hint: Dual legitimacy · winner take all · fixed terms.

cards.front: How does **Cheibub** (2007) rebut Linz?
cards.back: He argues the **society**, not the institution, is the problem: presidential systems tend to exist in societies where democracy of any type is unstable, so the correlation is spurious. Semi presidentialism is empirically **no less stable than parliamentarism**, provided the president cannot sack the PM.

cards.front: What is **judicial review**?
cards.back: The power of courts to strike down a law as **unconstitutional**, making the judiciary a **veto player** and a check on the majority.

cards.front: Why is judicial review controversial?
cards.back: Because it lets **unelected judges override elected majorities**. Defenders (Dahl) note judges are appointed by elected officials and courts claim to protect minorities.

cards.front: What did **Tate and Vallinder** name the trend of courts entering ever more political fights?
cards.back: The **judicialisation of politics**.

cards.front: How do common law and code law differ in judicial review?
cards.back: 1) **Common law** (Britain and its colonies, including the US): judges **follow precedent** → **decentralised and concrete** review, so any court can rule inside a real case. 2) **Code law** (Roman, Napoleon; French and Iberian colonies): a written **code** is supreme and precedent ignored → **centralised and abstract** review by one constitutional court.

cards.front: Which legal family produces decentralised, concrete review where any court can rule inside a real case?
cards.back: **Common law**, built on **precedent**.

cards.front: Why does a professional bureaucracy create a **principal agent problem**?
cards.back: Merit based **professionalisation** gives bureaucrats **expertise**, which is their own independent power. So the **agents** (officials) can pursue their own interests rather than the **principal's** (elected leaders and the public), causing inefficiency or corruption such as expanding budgets or taking bribes.

cards.front: What is an **iron triangle**?
cards.back: A closed policy loop of **bureaucrats, legislators, and business** in one sector that serves insiders and keeps outsiders out.

cards.front: What is the Japanese practice of officials taking jobs in firms they once regulated?
cards.back: **Amakudari** (descent from heaven).

cards.front: What is **New Public Management** (NPM)?
cards.back: A 1980s reform (Reagan, Thatcher) that imported **markets, competition, and customer satisfaction** into government.

cards.front: What did a UK study find about New Public Management's results?
cards.back: A **one third staff cut** but slightly **higher costs** and slightly **worse, less fair service**.
cards.hint: Fewer staff, but costlier and worse.

cards.front: How do unitary and federal systems differ on sovereignty?
cards.back: 1) **Unitary** (France, UK, Denmark): the centre holds **sole sovereignty**, and local powers are **delegated and revocable**. 2) **Federal** (US, Germany): sovereignty is **constitutionally shared** with subunits, which limits majorities, protects minorities, and adds veto players.

cards.front: What is federalism called when all subunits have equal powers?
cards.back: **Symmetrical** federalism (example: US).

cards.front: What is federalism called when some subunits get special powers?
cards.back: **Asymmetrical** federalism.

cards.front: What is reversible decentralisation within a unitary state called?
cards.back: **Devolution** (example: UK to Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland).

cards.front: What did **Riker** argue about federalism's stability?
cards.back: It is inherently **unstable**, tending toward either centralisation or secession.

cards.front: What makes federalism real in practice rather than only on paper?
cards.back: The **politics behind it**: 1) **revenue control** and 2) **upper house strength**, not paper rules. The **US Senate** is strong, the German **Bundesrat** weak. Mexico's **PRI** centralised a paper federal state; **Russia** is a federal shell after Putin gutted regional autonomy.
cards.hint: Revenue + upper house = the reality test.

cards.front: Match each case to its one line lesson: USA, Brazil, France, Russia, Japan.
cards.back: 1) **USA:** presidential separation of powers plus weak parties → gridlock. 2) **Brazil:** coalitional presidentialism, strong formal powers but ineffective. 3) **France:** semi presidential done right, cohabitation works. 4) **Russia:** semi presidential gone dominant → electoral authoritarianism. 5) **Japan:** bureaucratic power via iron triangles and amakudari.

cards.front: Give the two go to illustrations that the party system, not the constitution, drives how a government works.
cards.back: 1) **UK versus India:** same Westminster rules, but India's party system decides. Congress dominance made PMs less constrained; after 1989 coalitions forced constant bargaining (3 PMs in 30 years, then 12). 2) **Thatcher versus Reagan:** with a compliant majority Thatcher reshaped economic policy far more than Reagan, who faced a hostile Congress.
cards.hint: UK vs India; Thatcher vs Reagan.

cards.front: Why do proportional democracies redistribute more than majoritarian ones (Iversen and Soskice)?
cards.back: With three classes (lower, middle, upper): 1) in a **proportional** system the **middle class allies with the lower class** to redistribute from the rich → bigger welfare states. 2) In a **majoritarian** system the middle class allies with the **upper class** to avoid heavy taxes → less redistribution.
cards.hint: Which class does the middle class ally with?

cards.front: What reusable template classifies and evaluates any system of government?
cards.back: 1) **How is the executive chosen?** Parliament, direct election, or elected president plus PM. 2) **How is it removed?** No confidence, impeachment, or mixed. 3) **How many veto players?** Place it on Lijphart's majoritarian to consensus line. 4) **What is the trade off?** Weigh accountability, policymaking, and stability (Linz versus Cheibub). Always add: rules do not equal outcomes.
cards.hint: Chosen → removed → veto players → trade off.
